result.relation_rationale: The reported primary radiographic progression-free survival result matches the requested event set and time origin: randomization to radiographic progression or death from any cause. The article specifies CT/MRI assessment of soft-tissue lesions by RECIST 1.1 and bone scan assessment using PCWG2 criteria; the supplement gives the radiographic progression-free survival bone-scan criteria. questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the sequence method. A truncated search does not establish that the method is absent.

one group in the assessment of radiographic

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

sections.excerpt: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

38|BACKGROUND
39|Abiraterone acetate, a drug that blocks endogenous androgen synthesis, plus predni-
40|sone is indicated for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. We evaluated the
41|clinical benefit of abiraterone acetate plus prednisone with androgen-deprivation ther
42|apy in patients with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer.
43|METHODS
44|In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 1199 pa-
45|tients to receive either androgen-deprivation therapy plus abiraterone acetate (1000 mg
46|daily, given once daily as four 250-mg tablets) plus prednisone (5 mg daily) (the
47|abiraterone group) or androgen-deprivation therapy plus dual placebos (the placebo
48|group). The two primary end points were overall survival and radiographic progression-
49|free survival.
50|RESULTS
51|After a median follow-up of 30.4 months at a planned interim analysis (after 406 pa-
52|tients had died), the median overall survival was significantly longer in the abiraterone
53|group than in the placebo group (not reached vs. 34.7 months) (hazard ratio for death,
54|0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The median length of radio-
55|graphic progression-free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone group and 14.8
56|months in the placebo group (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.47; 95%
57|CI, 0.39 to 0.55; P<0.001). Significantly better outcomes in all secondary end points
58|were observed in the abiraterone group, including the time until pain progression, next
59|subsequent therapy for prostate cancer, initiation of chemotherapy, and prostate-
60|specific antigen progression (P<0.001 for all comparisons), along with next symptom-
61|atic skeletal events (P = 0.009). These findings led to the unanimous recommendation
62|by the independent data and safety monitoring committee that the trial be unblinded
63|and crossover be allowed for patients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone. Rates
64|of grade 3 hypertension and hypokalemia were higher in the abiraterone group.
65|CONCLUSIONS
66|The addition of abiraterone acetate and prednisone to androgen-deprivation therapy
67|significantly increased overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival in
68|men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer. (Funded
69|by Janssen Research and Development; LATITUDE ClinicalTrials.gov number,
70|NCT01715285.)

3|Abiraterone plus Prednisone in Prostate Cancer
4|M
5|etastatic, castration-sensitive
6|prostate cancer accounts for approxi-
7|mately 3% of all new prostate-cancer
8|diagnoses in the United States.1 Historically,
9|androgen-deprivation therapy consisting of bilat-
10|eral orchiectomy or luteinizing hormone-releas-
11|ing hormone analogues, with or without first-
12|generation androgen-receptor inhibitors, has been
13|the standard of care.2 Although the majority of
14|patients have an initial response to androgen-
15|deprivation therapy, most men with metastases
16|have progression to castration-resistant prostate
17|cancer within a median of approximately 1 year.3-5
18|Resistance to androgen-deprivation therapy is
19|largely driven by the reactivation of androgen-
20|receptor signaling through persistent adrenal an-
21|drogen production, up-regulation of intratumoral
22|testosterone production, modification of the bi-
23|ologic characteristics of androgen receptors, and
24|steroidogenic parallel pathways.2
25|The clinical benefit of adding docetaxel to
26|androgen-deprivation therapy versus treatment
27|with androgen-deprivation therapy alone has been
28|shown in three randomized, phase 3 trials -
29|Chemohormonal Therapy Versus Androgen Ab-
30|lation Randomized Trial for Extensive Disease in
31|Prostate Cancer (CHAARTED),5,6 Systemic Ther-
32|apy in Advancing or Metastatic Prostate Cancer:
33|Evaluation of Drug Efficacy (STAMPEDE),7 and
34|GETUG-153,8 - which collectively included more
35|than 3000 men with metastatic, castration-sensi-
36|tive prostate cancer. Androgen-deprivation ther-
37|apy plus docetaxel is now a standard of care for
38|men with metastatic, castration-sensitive pros-
39|tate cancer who are eligible for chemotherapy,
40|particularly those with a high metastatic burden,
41|as defined in the respective studies.9-11 Barriers
42|to the use of docetaxel include advanced patient
43|age, poor performance status, coexisting illness-
44|es, and patient preferences.9,12 Retrospective analy-
45|ses exploring real-world practice patterns13,14 indi-
46|cate that men with newly diagnosed, metastatic,
47|castration-sensitive prostate cancer who are not
48|being treated in clinical trials may be nearly a
49|decade older than those treated in clinical trials.
50|The concern with respect to chemotherapy-related
51|toxicity and the effect of coexisting illnesses on
52|complications is based on the severity of the
53|toxicity that has been observed. Chemotherapy-
54|related deaths were documented in all three
55|randomized trials in which docetaxel was added
56|to androgen-deprivation therapy.3,5,7
57|Abiraterone acetate, the prodrug of abiraterone,
58|inhibits cytochrome P-450c17, a critical enzyme
59|in androgen biosynthesis.15,16 Recent studies im-
60|plicate its active D4A metabolite in antitumor
61|effects, presumably through blockade of multi-
62|ple steroidogenic enzymes and antagonism of the
63|androgen receptor.17 Abiraterone acetate (here-
64|after referred to as abiraterone) in combination
65|with prednisone has been shown to significantly
66|increase overall survival and provide additional
67|clinical benefits in patients with metastatic,
68|castration-resistant prostate cancer who have
69|not received chemotherapy and in those who
70|have received previous docetaxel.18-22 The combi-
71|nation of abiraterone plus prednisone and andro-
72|gen-deprivation therapy has been shown to reduce
73|tumor burden in men with high-risk, localized
74|prostate cancer who are receiving neoadjuvant
75|therapy, which suggests a potential role for
76|inhibiting extragonadal androgen biosynthesis
77|before the emergence of castration resistance in
78|men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-
79|sensitive prostate cancer.23,24 In LATITUDE, a
80|multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-
81|controlled, phase 3 trial, we evaluated the addition
82|of abiraterone plus prednisone to androgen-
83|deprivation therapy, as compared with androgen-
84|deprivation therapy and dual placebos, on overall
85|survival, radiographic progression-free survival,
86|and clinically relevant measures in men with
87|newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive
88|prostate cancer.
89|Methods
90|Trial Design and Conduct
91|The trial was conducted at 235 sites in 34 coun-
92|tries in Europe, the Asia-Pacific region, Latin
93|America, and Canada. The trial protocol (avail-
94|able with the full text of this article at NEJM.org)
95|was approved by the review board at each par-
96|ticipating institution. The trial was conducted
97|according to the principles of the Declaration of
98|Helsinki and the International Conference on
99|Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice Guide-
100|lines. All the patients provided written informed
101|consent.
102|An independent data and safety monitoring
103|committee was commissioned by the sponsor,
104|Janssen Research and Development, to review
105|safety data on a regular basis and review effi-
106|cacy data at planned interim analyses. The trial

20|Patients and Treatments
21|Eligible patients were required to be at least 18
22|years of age and to have an Eastern Cooperative
23|Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status
24|score of 0 to 2 (on a 5-point scale, with higher
25|numbers indicating greater disability) with new-
26|ly diagnosed (≤3 months before randomization),
27|pathologically confirmed prostate cancer with-
28|out neuroendocrine differentiation or small-cell
29|histologic features. All the patients had high-risk,
30|metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer,
31|as documented by a positive bone scan or meta-
32|static lesions at the time of diagnosis on com-
33|puted tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance
34|imaging (MRI), according to Response Evaluation
35|Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), version 1.1.
36|In addition, the patients were required to have at
37|least two of the three following high-risk factors
38|associated with poor prognosis: a Gleason score
39|of 8 or more (on a scale of 2 to 10, with higher
40|scores indicating more aggressive disease), at
41|least three bone lesions, and the presence of
42|measurable visceral metastasis. Patients were
43|excluded if they had received previous chemo-
44|therapy, radiation therapy, or surgery for meta-
45|static prostate cancer, with the exception of
46|3 months or less of androgen-deprivation ther
47|apy with luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone
48|analogues or orchiectomy with or without con-
49|current first-generation androgen-receptor antag-
50|onists before baseline or one course of palliative
51|radiation or surgical therapy to treat symptoms
52|associated with metastatic disease.
53|Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
54|to receive androgen-deprivation therapy and abira
55|terone acetate (1000 mg daily, given once daily
56|as four 250-mg tablets) and prednisone (5 mg
57|daily) (the abiraterone group) or androgen-depri-
58|vation therapy and placebos (the placebo group).
59|Patients were stratified according to the presence
60|or absence of measurable visceral disease and
61|ECOG performance-status score (0 or 1 vs. 2).
62|Abiraterone or placebo was administered at least
63|1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal. All the
64|patients who had not undergone surgical castra-
65|tion received ongoing androgen-deprivation ther-
66|apy to reach or maintain a serum testosterone
67|level of less than 50 ng per deciliter (1.7 nmol
68|per liter). Safety and dosing adherence were
69|evaluated during each trial visit, at treatment
70|discontinuation (if applicable), and at the end-of-
71|trial visit.
72|End Points
73|The two primary efficacy end points were overall
74|survival and radiographic progression-free sur-
75|vival. Overall survival was defined as the time
76|from randomization to death from any cause,
77|and radiographic progression-free survival as the
78|time from randomization to the occurrence of
79|radiographic progression or death from any
80|cause. Radiographic progression of soft-tissue
81|lesions was evaluated by either CT or MRI on the
82|basis of RECIST, version 1.1. Progression on
83|bone scanning was assessed by adaptation of
84|Prostate Cancer Working Group 2 criteria (Table
85|S1 in the Supplementary Appendix, available at
86|NEJM.org).25 Potential bias favoring the abirater
87|one group in the assessment of radiographic
88|progression by investigators was audited with the
89|use of the method of the Pharmaceutical Re-
90|search and Manufacturers Association26 in a sam-
91|ple of 202 randomly selected patients with blind-
92|ed central review.
93|Prespecified secondary end points were the
94|time to the next "skeletal-related event" (described
95|here as a "symptomatic skeletal event," which
96|was defined as a clinical or pathological frac-
97|ture, spinal-cord compression, palliative radia-
98|tion to bone, or surgery involving bone), time to
99|progression with respect to prostate-specific
100|antigen (PSA) level on the basis of Prostate Can-
101|cer Working Group 2 criteria,25 time to the next
102|therapy for prostate cancer, time to initiation of
103|chemotherapy, and time to pain progression.

4|Pain progression was defined as an increase of
5|at least 30% from baseline in the worst pain
6|category on the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
7|as observed at two consecutive evaluations per-
8|formed at least 4 weeks apart.
9|Assessments
10|Efficacy assessments included sequential radio-
11|graphic imaging to assess radiographic progres-
12|sion-free survival (CT or MRI and bone scan-
13|ning) performed every 4 months, starting at
14|week 16. PSA levels were measured at baseline,
15|monthly in the first year, and then every 2 months
16|until end-of-trial treatment. Patients underwent
17|serial monitoring of vital signs, serum hemato-
18|logic and chemical findings, liver-function tests,
19|and serum testosterone levels. Adverse events
20|were graded with the use of the Common Termi-
21|nology Criteria for Adverse Events of the Na-
22|tional Cancer Institute, version 4.0.
23|Statistical Analysis
24|The overall level of significance was 0.05, with
25|allocation between the two primary end points
26|of overall survival (0.049) and radiographic
27|progression-free survival (0.001) (Table S2 in
28|the Supplementary Appendix). For overall sur-
29|vival, 852 events were required at the final
30|analysis to detect a hazard ratio of 0.81 at a
31|two-tailed significance level of 0.049, with a
32|statistical power of 85%. An analysis of radio-
33|graphic progression-free survival was planned
34|when 565 progressions or deaths had been ob-
35|served, which would provide a statistical power
36|of 94% to detect a hazard ratio of 0.667 at a
37|two-tailed significance level of 0.001. Two in-
38|terim analyses were included (Table S2 in the
39|Supplementary Appendix). The overall survival
40|analyses incorporated the group sequential de-
41|sign with an alpha spending function that was
42|calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power boundaries
43|of shape parameter 0.2 (which shape the prob-
44|ability distribution). Secondary end points were
45|tested with the use of the Hochberg test proce-
46|dure to control the familywise type I error rate.
47|The primary statistical method of comparison
48|for time-to-event end points was the stratified
49|log-rank test, according to the stratification
50|factors. The Cox proportional-hazards model
51|was used to estimate the hazard ratio and its
52|associated 95% confidence interval.
53|Results
54|Patients and Treatments
55|A total of 1199 patients underwent randomiza-
56|tion from February 12, 2013, through December
57|11, 2014. Of these patients, 597 were assigned to
58|the abiraterone group and 602 to the placebo
59|group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
60|The baseline demographic and disease charac-
61|teristics were well balanced between the two
62|groups (Table S3 in the Supplementary Appen-
63|dix). The results presented here are based on the
64|clinical cutoff date of October 31, 2016, for the
65|first interim analysis of overall survival, at which
66|time 406 deaths and 593 radiographic progres-
67|sions or deaths had occurred. At a median follow-
68|up of 30.4 months, the median time that the

46|(Table 2).
47|Discussion
48|In this phase 3 trial involving men with high-
49|risk, newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-
50|sensitive prostate cancer, the rate of overall
51|survival was significantly higher among those
52|who received androgen-deprivation therapy plus
53|abiraterone and prednisone than among those
54|who received androgen-deprivation therapy plus
55|placebos, with a 38% lower relative risk of death
56|(hazard ratio, 0.62) in the abiraterone group.
57|The addition of abiraterone plus prednisone to
58|androgen-deprivation therapy also significantly
59|prolonged radiographic progression-free survival
60|(hazard ratio, 0.47) and all secondary end points.
61|Since the between-group difference for overall
62|survival was significant at the time of the first
63|interim analysis and unblinding of the trial, this
64|analysis is considered to be final.

Our data support the hypoth- 9|esis that more effective inhibition of androgen- 10|receptor signaling as a component of the initial 11|systemic therapy in patients with castration- 12|sensitive prostate cancer leads to improved out- 13|comes. The clinical benefit that we observed con- 14|trasts with that from the many previous attempts 15|with castration and first-generation androgen- 16|receptor inhibitors,27,28 which showed only a 17|small improvement with a combined androgen- 18|blockade approach,29 presumably owing to the 19|lower potency and partial agonist activity of 20|these drugs. Several other ongoing randomized, 21|phase 3 trials in this patient population are ex- 22|amining androgen receptor-signaling combina- 23|tion therapies with androgen-deprivation ther 24|apy (Table S7 in the Supplementary Appendix) 25|and are exploring whether these treatments can 26|be added to androgen-deprivation therapy plus 27|docetaxel in patients with metastatic, castration- 28|sensitive prostate cancer. The assessment of effi- 29|cacy of subsequent therapies, including the types 30|of disease progression in patients who were re- 31|ceiving treatment, will require more long-term 32|analysis. 33|Men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castra- 34|tion-sensitive prostate cancer can have variable 35|outcomes, so we purposely enrolled those who 36|were considered to have at least two high-risk 37|prognostic features (e.g., a Gleason score of ≥8, 38|the presence of ≥3 bone lesions, or the presence 39|of measurable visceral metastasis),30-33 all of which 40|are associated with poor survival. In addition, 41|50% of the patients had symptomatic disease at 42|baseline. The patient population appears to be 43|similar to high-burden disease populations in 44|the three randomized trials that evaluated andro- 45|gen-deprivation therapy plus docetaxel,3,5,7 since 46|the outcomes in the control groups were similar 47|across those studies. After a median follow-up 48|of 7 years in GETUG-15, a nonsignificant 22% 49|reduction in the relative risk of death was ob- 50|served in patients with high-volume disease.8 A 51|significant 27% reduction in the relative risk of 52|death (and a reduction of 37% in patients with 53|high-volume disease) with androgen-deprivation 54|therapy plus docetaxel was observed after a 53.7- 55|month follow-up (approximately 50% of deaths) 56|in CHAARTED.6 In STAMPEDE, a significant 24% 57|risk reduction in death was observed among pa- 58|tients with metastatic, castration-sensitive pros- 59|tate cancer.7 (The STAMPEDE investigators now 60|report in the Journal the results of another trial 61|of abiraterone plus prednisone in men with local 62|ly advanced or metastatic prostate cancer.34) In 63|our trial, the efficacy of abiraterone, with a 38% 64|reduction in the risk of death among patients 65|who had not received previous treatment for 66|metastatic disease, compares favorably with pre- 67|vious findings. answer_anchors.text: Remote or central allocation was controlled by an independent external unit, or appropriate envelopes/containers were used.
The enrolling investigator or participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

questions.bias_construct: Whether the allocation sequence was concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned.
considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.

Keep concealment separate from sequence generation (how the sequence was made) and baseline imbalance (what the randomized groups look like). A random sequence or balanced baseline table does not establish concealment.
The reported sequence-generation method does not establish concealment.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the allocation safeguards. A truncated search does not establish that concealment details are absent.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes for remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel, or appropriately used opaque sequentially numbered sealed envelopes or identical sequentially numbered drug containers. Answer no when the enrolling investigator or participant could know the forthcoming allocation.
evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.2
questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned to interventions?

answer_anchors.text: Baseline imbalance indicates a problem with the randomization process.
No imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance.
No useful baseline information is available.

questions.bias_construct: Whether baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with randomization.
considerations: A few statistically significant differences at the conventional 0.05 threshold are usually compatible with chance.

This is a question about baseline imbalance suggesting a randomization problem, not about how the sequence was generated or whether allocation was concealed. Do not use the baseline table to backfill either process question.
This answer must not alter answers about sequence generation or concealment.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when no imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance. Answer yes for substantial group-size differences, an excess of statistically significant baseline differences beyond chance, a key prognostic imbalance very unlikely due to chance and large enough to bias the estimate, or excessive similarity incompatible with chance.
evidence_needed: Baseline characteristics for the randomized groups, intended allocation ratio, prognostic factors, and outcome baseline measures.
invalid_shortcuts: statistical significance of one isolated comparison
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when no useful baseline information is available, for example in an abstract or when only final-analysis participants are described.
questions.official_guidance: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

Patients and Treatments
Eligible patients were required to be at least 18
years of age and to have an Eastern Cooperative
Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status
score of 0 to 2 (on a 5-point scale, with higher
numbers indicating greater disability) with new-
ly diagnosed (≤3 months before randomization),
pathologically confirmed prostate cancer with-
out neuroendocrine differentiation or small-cell
histologic features. All the patients had high-risk,
metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer,
as documented by a positive bone scan or meta-
static lesions at the time of diagnosis on com-
puted tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI), according to Response Evaluation
Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), version 1.1.
In addition, the patients were required to have at
least two of the three following high-risk factors
associated with poor prognosis: a Gleason score
of 8 or more (on a scale of 2 to 10, with higher
scores indicating more aggressive disease), at
least three bone lesions, and the presence of
measurable visceral metastasis. Patients were
excluded if they had received previous chemo-
therapy, radiation therapy, or surgery for meta-
static prostate cancer, with the exception of
3 months or less of androgen-deprivation ther
apy with luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone
analogues or orchiectomy with or without con-
current first-generation androgen-receptor antag-
onists before baseline or one course of palliative
radiation or surgical therapy to treat symptoms
associated with metastatic disease.
Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive androgen-deprivation therapy and abira
terone acetate (1000 mg daily, given once daily
as four 250-mg tablets) and prednisone (5 mg
daily) (the abiraterone group) or androgen-depri-
vation therapy and placebos (the placebo group).
Patients were stratified according to the presence
or absence of measurable visceral disease and
ECOG performance-status score (0 or 1 vs. 2).

Primary Endpoint
The primary efficacy endpoint is overall survival defined as the time from randomization to date
of death from any cause.
Secondary Endpoints

Radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) based on Prostate Cancer Working Group 2
(PCWG2) and modified RECIST as the time from randomization to the occurrence of one of
the following:

A subject is considered to have progressed by bone scan if the first bone scan with
≥2 new lesions compared to baseline is observed ≥16 weeks (Cycle 5 Day 1) from
randomization. If the ≥2 new lesions are noted at or before Cycle 5 Day 1, a
confirmatory bone scan will be performed ≥6 weeks later (to eliminate a false
progression that could potentially be a flare phenomenon).

Progression of soft tissue lesions measured by CT or MRI as defined in modified
RECIST criteria

Death from any cause

In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 1199 pa-

daily, given once daily as four 250-mg tablets) plus prednisone (5 mg daily) (the
abiraterone group) or androgen-deprivation therapy plus dual placebos (the placebo
group). The two primary end points were overall survival and radiographic progression-
free survival.

After a median follow-up of 30.4 months at a planned interim analysis (after 406 pa-

by an independent statistician not otherwise involved with this study, and will be implemented
within a global interactive web or voice response system (IWRS/IVRS).

evidence.quote:
Patients and Treatments
Eligible patients were required to be at least 18
years of age and to have an Eastern Cooperative
Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status
score of 0 to 2 (on a 5-point scale, with higher
numbers indicating greater disability) with new-
ly diagnosed (≤3 months before randomization),
pathologically confirmed prostate cancer with-
out neuroendocrine differentiation or small-cell
histologic features. All the patients had high-risk,
metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer,
as documented by a positive bone scan or meta-
static lesions at the time of diagnosis on com-
puted tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI), according to Response Evaluation
Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), version 1.1.
In addition, the patients were required to have at
least two of the three following high-risk factors
associated with poor prognosis: a Gleason score
of 8 or more (on a scale of 2 to 10, with higher
scores indicating more aggressive disease), at
least three bone lesions, and the presence of
measurable visceral metastasis. Patients were
excluded if they had received previous chemo-
therapy, radiation therapy, or surgery for meta-
static prostate cancer, with the exception of
3 months or less of androgen-deprivation ther
apy with luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone
analogues or orchiectomy with or without con-
current first-generation androgen-receptor antag-
onists before baseline or one course of palliative
radiation or surgical therapy to treat symptoms
associated with metastatic disease.
Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive androgen-deprivation therapy and abira
terone acetate (1000 mg daily, given once daily
as four 250-mg tablets) and prednisone (5 mg
daily) (the abiraterone group) or androgen-depri-
vation therapy and placebos (the placebo group).
Patients were stratified according to the presence
or absence of measurable visceral disease and
ECOG performance-status score (0 or 1 vs. 2).

9.2.2.
Endpoints
Primary Endpoint
The primary efficacy endpoint is overall survival defined as the time from randomization to date
of death from any cause.
Secondary Endpoints

Radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) based on Prostate Cancer Working Group 2
(PCWG2) and modified RECIST as the time from randomization to the occurrence of one of
the following:

A subject is considered to have progressed by bone scan if the first bone scan with

answers.justification: The report describes a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, and the protocol states that participants were intended to remain blinded. The evaluated result uses data cut off on October 31, 2016; the committee recommended unblinding on January 12, 2017, after that cutoff. Although hypertension and hypokalemia were more frequent with abiraterone, the report does not say participants recognized these as assignment-specific before the result cutoff. This supports probably no for awareness during the period contributing to this result.
unknowns: The report does not describe a formal assessment of whether participants guessed their assignments before the cutoff.

counterevidence.implication: Hypertension and hypokalemia occurred more often with abiraterone and could have weakened blinding, but the report does not establish that participants knew these effects identified their assigned treatment.

answers.justification: The published report calls the trial double-blind and placebo-controlled. The protocol states that study-site, sponsor, and CRO team members were intended to remain blinded, apart from defined independent safety and monitoring exceptions. The recommended trial unblinding followed the October 31, 2016 data cutoff for this result. The evidence supports probably no for the personnel involved in care and assessment during the period contributing to the result.
unknowns: The report does not document whether any site personnel were inadvertently unblinded before the data cutoff.

questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

answer_anchors.text: Outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
Outcome data were not available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
The report provides no information about the extent of missing outcome data.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Neutral paired control: complete ascertainment and an analysis denominator with unresolved ascertainment differ only in the availability premise; administrative censoring and worsening-related follow-up loss differ only in the missingness mechanism.
invalid_shortcuts: analysis denominators or ITT membership alone

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

questions.decision_rule: Evidence may come from methods correcting for bias or sensitivity analyses showing little change under plausible assumptions about missingness and true outcome. evidence.quote:
Patients and Treatments
Eligible patients were required to be at least 18
years of age and to have an Eastern Cooperative
Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status
score of 0 to 2 (on a 5-point scale, with higher
numbers indicating greater disability) with new-
ly diagnosed (≤3 months before randomization),
pathologically confirmed prostate cancer with-
out neuroendocrine differentiation or small-cell
histologic features. All the patients had high-risk,
metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer,
as documented by a positive bone scan or meta-
static lesions at the time of diagnosis on com-
puted tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI), according to Response Evaluation
Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), version 1.1.
In addition, the patients were required to have at
least two of the three following high-risk factors
associated with poor prognosis: a Gleason score
of 8 or more (on a scale of 2 to 10, with higher
scores indicating more aggressive disease), at
least three bone lesions, and the presence of
measurable visceral metastasis. Patients were
excluded if they had received previous chemo-
therapy, radiation therapy, or surgery for meta-
static prostate cancer, with the exception of
3 months or less of androgen-deprivation ther
apy with luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone
analogues or orchiectomy with or without con-
current first-generation androgen-receptor antag-
onists before baseline or one course of palliative
radiation or surgical therapy to treat symptoms
associated with metastatic disease.
Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive androgen-deprivation therapy and abira
terone acetate (1000 mg daily, given once daily
as four 250-mg tablets) and prednisone (5 mg
daily) (the abiraterone group) or androgen-depri-
vation therapy and placebos (the placebo group).
Patients were stratified according to the presence
or absence of measurable visceral disease and
ECOG performance-status score (0 or 1 vs. 2).

Endpoints
Primary Endpoint
The primary efficacy endpoint is overall survival defined as the time from randomization to date
of death from any cause.
Secondary Endpoints

Radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) based on Prostate Cancer Working Group 2
(PCWG2) and modified RECIST as the time from randomization to the occurrence of one of
the following:

A subject is considered to have progressed by bone scan if the first bone scan with
≥2 new lesions compared to baseline is observed ≥16 weeks (Cycle 5 Day 1) from
randomization. If the ≥2 new lesions are noted at or before Cycle 5 Day 1, a
confirmatory bone scan will be performed ≥6 weeks later (to eliminate a false
progression that could potentially be a flare phenomenon).

Progression of soft tissue lesions measured by CT or MRI as defined in modified
RECIST criteria

Death from any cause

11
Supplementary Table S1. Radiographic Progression-free Survival Definition per
RECIST Version 1.1 as Adapted by Prostate Cancer Working Group 2 Criteria.
•
Patients who had ≥2 new bone lesions on 16-week scans, with confirmatory
scans performed 6 or more weeks later
o
Patients with confirmatory scans that showed ≥2 new lesions
compared with 16-week scans (i.e., total of four new lesions
compared with baseline scan) were considered to have disease
progression by bone scan
o
Patients who on confirmatory scans did not show ≥2 new
lesions compared with 16-week scans were not considered to
have disease progression at that time. All subsequent scans
served as "confirmatory scans" and were considered to show
disease progression with ≥2 new lesions compared with 16-
week scans
•
Patients who did not have ≥2 new bone lesions on 16-week scans did not
require a confirmatory scan. For any subsequent scan beyond 16 weeks, the
first scan that would show ≥2 new lesions compared with baseline scans was
considered to demonstrate disease progression by bone scan
RECIST denotes Response Evaluation Criteria In Solid Tumors.

In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 1199 pa-
tients to receive either androgen-deprivation therapy plus abiraterone acetate (1000 mg
daily, given once daily as four 250-mg tablets) plus prednisone (5 mg daily) (the
abiraterone group) or androgen-deprivation therapy plus dual placebos (the placebo
group). The two primary end points were overall survival and radiographic progression-
free survival.
RESULTS
After a median follow-up of 30.4 months at a planned interim analysis (after 406 pa-
tients had died), the median overall survival was significantly longer in the abiraterone
group than in the placebo group (not reached vs. 34.7 months) (hazard ratio for death,
0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The median length of radio-
graphic progression-free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone group and 14.8
months in the placebo group (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.47; 95%
CI, 0.39 to 0.55; P<0.001). Significantly better outcomes in all secondary end points

# Assess missing outcome data

Use this reference for Domain 3. The approved Result fixes the outcome and time
point; the returned question cards fix answer direction and activation.

Every active answer is accompanied by a concise justification, an `unknowns`
array (use `[]` when none are identified), and a `counterevidence` array. A
counterpoint refers to the answer's zero-based basis index, for example:

```json
"counterevidence": [{"basis_index": 0, "implication": "This passage limits the strength of the selected answer."}]
```

Inactive branch answers may be omitted or retained without fabricated reasoning;
the server commits only the dependency-closed active path.

## Availability audit

For D3.1, support Yes or Probably Yes with actual outcome-availability
evidence. Accept one or more of:

- comparable observed-outcome counts for the randomized population;
- arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring rates, reasons, and follow-up
  accounting; or
- an explicit statement that ascertainment was complete or nearly complete.

Support No or Probably No with evidence that availability was materially
incomplete for this Result. If the extent remains unknown after bounded
retrieval, use No information. Failure to demonstrate complete availability is
not evidence that availability was incomplete.

The following do not establish affirmative availability on their own:

- analysis denominators or ITT membership;
- planned or scheduled follow-up;
- treatment continuation or discontinuation; or
- a generic censoring rule without actual rates or follow-up accounting.

For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later
time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not
establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect
outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their
outcome and time window to the approved Result. Recovery may inform bias from
missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

When the availability premise remains unresolved, use the active comparison
card's full Source inventory to inspect unopened supplements or combined
protocol documents. Search for concrete study wording such as the outcome
status, withdrawal or loss-to-follow-up labels, and the reported time point;
`missing outcome data` alone may not occur in the report. Widen the Source
scope or continue a cached cursor only as needed, and stop when comparable
observed counts or complete follow-up accounting are inspected. If the
captured Sources and bounded page windows do not establish availability,
document that limit instead of treating an empty Source group or a no-hit
search as evidence of missing outcomes.

## Reconcile availability

Keep these quantities distinct for each arm and time point:

- randomized participants;
- participants with the outcome observed;
- participants included in the reported analysis;
- participants whose outcomes were imputed; and
- post-randomization exclusions; and
- outcome events, which are a numerator rather than an observed-participant count.

An analyzed count is not necessarily an observed count. Imputed outcomes count
as missing outcome data for RoB 2. Treatment discontinuation is not missing
outcome data when follow-up and outcome ascertainment continued.

If some outcomes are missing, assess whether data remain available for nearly
all randomized participants. Keep the randomized denominator, outcome-observed
count, analyzed count, imputed count, excluded count, and event count separate
for the same arm, population, unit, and time point. Consider whether the
missing outcomes could make an important difference to this Result. For
dichotomous outcomes, compare the missing count with observed events, not only
the randomized denominator. A count below the randomized total does not settle
that question, and no universal percentage threshold replaces this impact
judgment.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring
caused by missing follow-up before the outcome could be observed. Treatment
discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that
outcome observation stopped. For time-to-event Results, censoring may still
create missing outcome information; assess its timing, reason, actual follow-up
pathway, and relation to treatment or prognosis instead of treating every
censored participant as either fully observed or missing by default.

Question 3.1 may include compact `missing_data` rows. Give each row a comparable
arm, population, unit, and time point. Use a row-level `basis` only to narrow or
add to the answer's Evidence. The server calculates differences and fractions
only after scopes match and preserves conflicting reports without choosing the
scientific answer.

When a count comparison would help before answering, call `get_domain_context`
with `missing_data` rows. Every preview row needs a nonempty `basis` containing
current-Trial Evidence references: no answer exists to supply inherited Evidence.
Inspect `comparison_cards[].missing_data`
for differences, fractions, and conflicting reports. The preview changes no
checkpoint or State revision. To retain the chosen rows, submit them with the
3.1 answer in `validate_domain_assessment`; omit row `basis` there only to reuse
the answer's Evidence when it supports those counts. After its receipt, save
the exact draft with `save_domain_judgment`.

Check each input against its source passage before using the arithmetic. The
helper subtracts supplied observed counts from randomized counts; it does not
extract counts or sum grouped departures. Keep unknown observed counts unknown.
Skip the preview when an explicit ascertainment statement resolves availability
without arithmetic.

When a row includes typed `semantics`, treat it as scope metadata, not as a
shortcut to a signalling answer. `event_count` is an event numerator and never
means that every participant's outcome was observed. `analyzed`, `safety`, and
`per_protocol` roles are denominators or populations, not availability. Keep
administrative censoring, loss to follow-up, treatment change, imputation, and
post-randomization exclusions as distinct facts. The server preserves these
fields and only derives `randomized - observed`; it does not decide whether a
censored participant is informative.

## Assess bias from missingness

If data were not available for all or nearly all participants, ask in sequence:

1. Does a bias-correcting method or informative sensitivity analysis show that
   the Result was not biased?
2. Could missingness depend on the true outcome, based on reasons, health
   status, withdrawal, loss to follow-up, or censoring?
3. If it could, is that dependence likely given arm differences, reasons,
   prognostic factors, or trial circumstances?

Simple imputation, including last observation carried forward or multiple
imputation based only on intervention group, does not by itself show freedom from
bias. A comparison that changes group attribution, such as ITT versus
as-treated, does not test unobserved outcome values unless the source establishes
that relationship. A reassuring sensitivity analysis must vary plausible
unobserved outcomes under the missingness mechanism relevant to the approved
Result. Documented reasons support reassurance only when they address the
outcome relationship.

Keep possible dependence in 3.3 separate from likely dependence in 3.4. For
3.4, state which reasons or trial circumstances support the likelihood judgment.
Absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likely dependence. Preserve
`no_information` when the card's uncertainty rule applies, even when that answer
leads to High risk of bias.

D3.2 does not allow `no_information`. When no bias-correcting evidence is found,
use the question card to choose a permitted negative or probably-negative answer
with the appropriate limitation or Evidence basis. Do not fabricate direct
support for the absence of bias.

## Paired premise check

Use neutral pairs to keep the seams separate: complete outcome ascertainment
versus an analysis denominator with unresolved availability; common administrative
censoring versus follow-up stopping after worsening symptoms. The changed premise
is the ascertainment or missingness mechanism, not a percentage threshold. The
pair supplies no answer or risk label; the host still grounds each proposition
in exact Evidence and retains No information or High where the official path
requires it.

progression if:
a.
the patient receives subsequent therapy (ie, cytotoxic chemotherapy) known or intended
for prostate cancer during the study prior to the radiographic progression;
b. the patient misses ≥2 consecutive planned radiographic scans or has ≥2 consecutive
unreadable scans (more than 35 weeks apart);
c.
the patient has unequivocal progression of non-bone non-target lesions (eg, appearance of
nonmeasurable visceral metastases or pathologically confirmed malignant effusions).
